lists.title: Persian A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Persian: pronouns with budan ("to be"), verb-final word order, personal verb endings, negation with na-/nemi-, adjectives after the noun, yes/no questions, the -ha plural, and the ra object marker.

lists.title: Persian A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Talking about the past: the two-stem system, simple past and its na- negation, the present perfect, habitual past with mi-, comparatives in -tar, object clitics on the verb, question words, light-verb compounds, and counting with ta.

lists.title: Persian B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Saying what might, must, and will happen: the be- subjunctive after khastan, bayad and shayad, tavanestan, the written future with khaham, real conditionals with agar, relative and reported clauses with ke, stacked ezafe chains, and infinitives used as nouns.

lists.title: Persian B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Depth and distance: the past perfect, unreal conditionals in the habitual past, the shodan passive, causatives in -andan, ta for purpose and until, and the gap between written miravam and spoken miram.

lists.title: Persian C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Register at the top of the range: administrative Persian with gardid, namud and mibashad, Arabic broken plurals like kotob and olama, and the literary past forms that fill older prose.

lists.title: Persian C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Near-native control: the conventions of classical verse, idiom and light-verb nuance, and shifting register between deferential, neutral, and intimate Persian.

points.title: Personal pronouns and budan ("to be")
points.function: Say who/what something is
points.explanation: Persian's "to be" changes with the subject just like English: man hastam ("I am"), to hasti ("you are"), oo ast ("he/she/it is"), ma hastim ("we are"). In casual speech ast often shortens to -e attached to the previous word, but the full است is standard written Persian.

drills.hint: am — 1st person singular of "to be"
are — 2nd person singular of "to be"
are — 1st person plural of "to be"

points.title: Verb-final word order (SOV)
points.function: Build a basic sentence in Persian order
points.explanation: Persian sentences are Subject-Object-Verb: the verb comes LAST, unlike English's Subject-Verb-Object. Man chai mikhaham, literally "I tea want," means "I want tea." Whatever else is in the sentence, the conjugated verb sits at the very end.

drills.hint: want — the verb comes at the very end
see — verb-final position
eat — verb at the very end

points.title: Personal verb endings: -am, -i, -ad
points.function: Conjugate a present-tense verb for its subject
points.explanation: Persian present-tense verbs take personal endings on the stem: -am (I), -i (you), -ad (he/she/it), -im (we), -id (you pl.), -and (they). Mikonam (I do) shares the same pattern as miravam (I go) → miravi (you go) → miravad (he/she/it goes) — same stem, different ending.

drills.hint: go — 2nd person singular, -ی ending
goes — 3rd person singular, -د ending
go — 1st person singular, -م ending

points.title: Negation with na- / nemi-
points.function: Say what you don't do or don't want
points.explanation: To negate a Persian verb, prefix نمی‌ (for the present tense) directly onto it: می‌دانم ("I know") → نمی‌دانم ("I don't know"); می‌خواهم ("I want") → نمی‌خواهم ("I don't want"). The negative prefix always attaches right before the verb.

drills.hint: don't know — نمی‌ prefixed onto می‌دانم
don't want — نمی‌ prefixed onto می‌خواهم
don't see — نمی‌ prefixed onto می‌بینم

points.title: Adjectives follow the noun
points.function: Put adjectives in the right place
points.explanation: Unlike English, Persian adjectives come AFTER the noun they describe: ketab khoob, literally "book good," means "a good book," not "good book" in English word order. There's a linking vowel between the two in speech (the ezafe), but with most consonant-final nouns like کتاب, nothing extra is written — the two words simply sit side by side.

drills.hint: good — placed AFTER the noun, not before
good — again, after the noun
big — adjective follows the noun

points.title: Yes/no questions: same word order, just a question mark
points.function: Ask a yes/no question without reordering the sentence
points.explanation: Persian doesn't invert word order or add a helper word to ask a yes/no question — spoken Persian just rises in pitch at the end, and written Persian adds a question mark: می‌روی؟ ("Are you going?") looks exactly like the statement می‌روی ("You're going") except for the ؟.

drills.hint: going — statement form, the question mark signals the question
going — same form as the statement
are — "to be," unchanged in form; only the ؟ makes it a question

points.title: The plural suffix -ha
points.function: Make a noun plural
points.explanation: The plural suffix -hâ attaches to a noun to make it plural: ketab ("book") → ketab-hâ ("books"). It's often written joined to the noun with a thin connector, but many typed texts write it as a separate word instead — both are common. Persian doesn't require a plural marker on every noun the way English does: after a number, the noun stays singular (se ketab = "three book," not "three books").

drills.hint: the plural suffix, often typed as a separate word
plural — same suffix
plural — same suffix

points.title: Ra marks a definite direct object
points.function: Mark a direct object you already know about
points.explanation: را is a postposition (it comes AFTER its noun) that marks a DEFINITE direct object — something specific you already know about: کتاب را می‌خوانم ("I'm reading THE book") vs. کتاب می‌خوانم ("I'm reading a book / reading in general"). An object left unmarked is indefinite or generic.

drills.hint: the definite object marker — a postposition, placed after the noun
the definite object marker
the definite object marker, standing after the noun

points.title: Possession with ezafe: ketab-e man
points.function: Say whose something is
points.explanation: Persian links a thing to its owner with the ezafe, an unwritten -e vowel between the two words: کتاب من is read ketab-e man, "the book of me" = "my book." Nothing is added in writing after a consonant — the words simply sit side by side, owner second. After a word ending in the silent ه the ezafe IS written, as a small hamza on top: خانهٔ من (khane-ye man, "my house").

drills.hint: the pronoun for the owner — "me," linked by the unwritten ezafe
the owner — "him/her"; the ezafe vowel is not written
the owner — "us"; the ezafe is written on خانه as a hamza
friend — the possessed thing comes FIRST, the owner second
teacher — the owner can be a noun, not just a pronoun

points.title: Possessive endings: -am, -at, -ash
points.function: Attach the owner straight onto the noun
points.explanation: Instead of a separate pronoun, Persian can hang the owner directly on the noun: -am (my), -at (your), -ash (his/her), -eman (our), -etan (your pl.), -eshan (their). کتاب becomes کتابم (ketabam, "my book"). It is the everyday equivalent of کتاب من. After the silent ه the ending is joined with a thin connector: خانه becomes خانه‌ام (khane-am).

drills.translation: My book is on the table.
drills.hint: my book — noun plus the -am ending, written as one word
your mother — noun plus the -at ending
his name — noun plus the -ash ending
my house — after the silent ه the ending joins with a thin connector
my friend — noun plus the -am ending

points.title: The verb dashtan ("to have")
points.function: Say what you have
points.explanation: داشتن ("to have") is conjugated دارم، داری، دارد، داریم، دارید، دارند. It is one of the few verbs that takes NO می‌ prefix in the present — دارم, never می‌دارم. The negative is built with ن‌ on the front: ندارم ("I don't have").

drills.hint: have — 1st person singular, and no می prefix on this verb
have — 2nd person singular
has — 3rd person singular
have — 1st person plural
don't have — the negative prefix ن, not نمی, on this verb

points.title: Simple past: the past stem
points.function: Say what happened
points.explanation: The past tense is built on the past stem, which is the infinitive minus its final ن: رفتن → رفت, دیدن → دید, خوردن → خورد. Add the personal endings straight onto it: رفتم (I went), رفتی (you went), رفت (he/she went), رفتیم، رفتید، رفتند. Note that the third person singular takes NO ending at all — the bare stem رفت already means "he went."

drills.hint: went — past stem plus the 1st person singular ending
went — past stem plus the 2nd person singular ending
went — 3rd person singular, the bare past stem with no ending

drills.translation: We saw a film last night.
drills.hint: saw — past stem of دیدن plus the 1st person plural ending
ate — past stem of خوردن plus the 1st person singular ending

points.title: Two verb stems: present and past
points.function: Pick the right stem for the tense
points.explanation: Every Persian verb has TWO stems, and they often look nothing alike: رفتن has رو in the present (می‌روم) and رفت in the past (رفتم); گفتن has گو and گفت; دیدن has بین and دید; خواندن has خوان and خواند. The past stem is always predictable (infinitive minus ن); the present stem has to be learned with the verb. Once you have the pair, everything else follows.

drills.hint: saw — the PAST stem of دیدن with the 1st person ending
see — the PRESENT stem of the same verb, with می
told — the past stem of گفتن; the present stem is گو

drills.translation: I read a book every day.
drills.hint: read — the present stem of خواندن, with می

drills.translation: Last night I read a book.
drills.hint: read — the past stem of the same verb

points.title: Past negation with na-
points.function: Say what didn't happen
points.explanation: Past verbs are negated with ن‌ on the front — NOT with نمی‌, which belongs to the present: رفتم → نرفتم ("I didn't go"), دیدم → ندیدم ("I didn't see"). The prefix goes before the past stem and the endings stay exactly the same.

drills.translation: I didn't go to school yesterday.
drills.hint: didn't go — the ن prefix on the past form
didn't see — ن plus the past of دیدن
didn't say — ن plus the past of گفتن, 1st person plural
didn't eat — ن plus the past of خوردن, 2nd person singular
didn't come — ن plus the past of آمدن

points.title: Present perfect: rafte-am
points.function: Report something already done
points.explanation: The present perfect pairs a past participle (past stem + ه: رفته، دیده، خورده) with short forms of "to be": رفته‌ام (I have gone), رفته‌ای، رفته است، رفته‌ایم، رفته‌اید، رفته‌اند. Like English "I have seen," it reports a past event whose result still matters now — which is why it is the natural tense for "have you ever…?"

drills.hint: have seen — participle joined to the 1st person short form of "to be"
gone — the participle; است carries the person here
have read — participle of خواندن, 1st person plural
have been/gone — participle, 2nd person singular
have eaten — participle of خوردن, 1st person singular

points.title: Comparatives and superlatives: -tar, -tarin
points.function: Compare two things, or pick the top one
points.explanation: Add ‌تر for "more" and ‌ترین for "most": بزرگ → بزرگ‌تر (bigger), بزرگ‌ترین (biggest). The comparison partner follows از ("than"): تهران از اصفهان بزرگ‌تر است. Word order differs between the two: a comparative FOLLOWS its noun, but a superlative goes BEFORE it — بزرگ‌ترین شهر ("the biggest city"). خوب has the irregular pair بهتر / بهترین, written solid.

drills.sentence: این کتاب از آن کتاب {{answer}} است.
drills.translation: This book is better than that book.
drills.hint: better — the irregular comparative of خوب
drills.transliteration: in ketab az an ketab behtar ast.

drills.hint: bigger — adjective plus the comparative suffix

drills.translation: My brother is younger than me.
drills.hint: smaller/younger — adjective plus the comparative suffix
best — irregular superlative, standing BEFORE the noun

drills.translation: This is the biggest city in Iran.
drills.hint: biggest — superlative suffix, and it comes before the noun

points.title: Object pronoun clitics: didamash
points.function: Recognize a pronoun object stuck on the verb
points.explanation: Instead of او را دیدم, Persian often hangs the object pronoun straight on the verb: دیدمش ("I saw him"), دیدمت ("I saw you"), دیدیمش ("we saw him"). The endings are the same set as the possessives — ـم، ـت، ـش، ـمان، ـتان، ـشان — but here they mean me/you/him, not my/your/his. Word order tells you which: on a noun they possess, on a verb they are the object.

drills.hint: I saw him — past verb with the 3rd person object stuck on the end
I saw you — same verb, 2nd person object clitic
I read it — past of خواندن with the object clitic
we saw him — 1st person plural verb plus the object clitic

points.title: Question words in a full sentence
points.function: Ask what, where, when and why
points.explanation: A Persian question word does not jump to the front the way English's does — it simply stands where the answer would stand, and the verb still comes last: تو کجا می‌روی؟ is literally "you where go?" The core set is کجا (where), کی (who; also when), چرا (why), چطور (how) and چه/چی (what), with چیست as the written "what is…?"

drills.hint: where — it stays in the middle; the verb is still last
why — placed before the verb, no reordering
who — one short word, before the verb
what is (it) — the written form that fuses "what" with "is"
how — asking after someone's state

points.title: Habitual past: miraftam
points.function: Say what you used to do
points.explanation: Put می‌ on a simple past and you get the habitual or ongoing past — English "used to go" or "was going": رفتم ("I went") → می‌رفتم ("I used to go"). It is the tense for routines, backgrounds and descriptions in a story. The negative is نمی‌: نمی‌رفتم.

drills.translation: I used to go to school every day.
drills.hint: used to go — می on the past form, 1st person singular
drills.transliteration: man har ruz be madrese miraftam.

drills.translation: He used to go to bed late every night.
drills.hint: used to sleep — می on the past of خوابیدن, 3rd person singular

drills.translation: Every summer we used to go to the north.
drills.hint: used to go — 1st person plural of the same tense
drills.transliteration: ma har tabestan be shomal miraftim.

drills.translation: You used to see him every day.
drills.hint: used to see — می on the past of دیدن, 2nd person singular
drills.transliteration: to har ruz u ra mididi.

drills.hint: didn't know — the negative of this tense, on the past of شناختن

points.title: Light-verb compounds: kar kardan, harf zadan
points.function: Use the compound verbs Persian builds everything from
points.explanation: Most everyday Persian verbs are two pieces: a fixed noun or adjective plus a light verb — کار کردن ("to work," literally "work do"), حرف زدن ("to speak," "word hit"), گوش دادن ("to listen," "ear give"), تماشا کردن ("to watch"). Only the light verb conjugates; the first piece never changes: کار می‌کنم، کار کردم، کار خواهم کرد.

drills.hint: do — only the light verb conjugates; کار stays put
hits — the light verb of "to speak," 3rd person singular
give — the light verb of "to listen," 1st person plural
the fixed noun half of the compound meaning "to watch"
the fixed noun half of the compound meaning "to work"

points.title: Numbers and the counter ta
points.function: Count things the Persian way
points.explanation: After a number the Persian noun stays SINGULAR: سه کتاب, literally "three book." In ordinary speech and writing a counter تا usually sits between the number and the noun for countable things: سه تا کتاب. The numbers themselves are یک، دو، سه، چهار، پنج، شش، هفت، هشت، نه، ده.

drills.hint: the counter word between a number and its noun
the same counter word
five — and note the noun after it stays singular
four — the number before the counter
two — the noun after it is not pluralized

points.title: The subjunctive: beravam
points.function: Say what you want, must or might do
points.explanation: For anything not presented as fact — a wish, an obligation, a possibility — Persian uses the subjunctive: بـ + present stem + endings, with NO می‌. رفتن gives بروم، بروی، برود. It follows می‌خواهم ("I want to…"), باید ("must"), شاید ("maybe") and similar: می‌خواهم بروم, باید بروم, شاید برود.

drills.hint: go — subjunctive after "I want": بـ prefix, no می
take — the light verb of "to learn," in the subjunctive after باید
come — subjunctive of آمدن after شاید

drills.translation: Do you want to drink tea?
drills.hint: eat/drink — subjunctive of خوردن, 2nd person singular
read — subjunctive of خواندن after باید

points.title: Future with khaham raft
points.function: Write about the future
points.explanation: Formal and written Persian marks the future with خواهم/خواهی/خواهد/خواهیم/خواهید/خواهند followed by the SHORT infinitive — the bare past stem, unchanged for person: خواهم رفت ("I will go"), خواهد آمد ("he will come"). Everyday speech simply uses the present tense with a time word (فردا می‌روم), so this pattern belongs mostly to writing and formal registers.

drills.translation: I will go to Tehran tomorrow.
drills.hint: will — the 1st person auxiliary; رفت stays bare after it
drills.transliteration: man farda be Tehran khaham raft.

drills.hint: will — the 3rd person singular auxiliary
will — the 1st person plural auxiliary
drills.transliteration: ma in ketab ra khahim khand.

drills.hint: go — the bare past stem after the auxiliary, with no ending
see — bare past stem, person is already on the auxiliary
drills.transliteration: man farda to ra khaham did.

points.title: Conditionals type 1: agar + subjunctive
points.function: Talk about a real possibility
points.explanation: For a condition that may well come true, اگر takes the SUBJUNCTIVE and the result clause stays in the ordinary present: اگر به تهران بروی، او را می‌بینی ("if you go to Tehran, you'll see him"). English uses a present tense in the if-clause; Persian uses the بـ form.

drills.sentence: اگر به تهران {{answer}}، او را می‌بینی.
drills.translation: If you go to Tehran, you'll see him.
drills.hint: go — subjunctive in the if-clause, 2nd person singular
drills.transliteration: agar be Tehran beravi, u ra mibini.

drills.sentence: اگر وقت داشته {{answer}}، به تو زنگ می‌زنم.
drills.translation: If I have time, I'll call you.
drills.hint: be — the subjunctive half of "to have" in a condition
drills.transliteration: agar vaght dashte basham, be to zang mizanam.

drills.translation: If it rains, we won't go.
drills.hint: come — subjunctive of آمدن; Persian says rain "comes"
read — subjunctive of خواندن, 2nd person singular
can — subjunctive of توانستن, 1st person singular

points.title: Relative clauses with ke
points.function: Add a which/who clause to a noun
points.explanation: که introduces every relative clause — it covers English who, which and that all at once, and it is never dropped. The noun it describes usually carries an indefinite ـی: مردی که دیدم ("the man I saw"), کتابی که خواندم ("the book I read"). The relative clause sits right after that noun, and its own verb still comes last.

drills.translation: The book I read was good.
drills.hint: the linker that opens the clause — never omitted, unlike English "that"

drills.translation: The man I saw was my friend.
drills.hint: was — the main verb, after the relative clause closes
drills.transliteration: mardi ke didam dust-e man bud.

drills.sentence: خانه‌ای که در آن زندگی می‌کنم بزرگ {{answer}}.
drills.translation: The house I live in is big.
drills.hint: is — the main clause verb, at the very end
drills.transliteration: khane-i ke dar an zendegi mikonam bozorg ast.

drills.translation: The woman sitting over there is a teacher.
drills.hint: the relative linker after the indefinite noun
drills.transliteration: zani ke anja neshaste moallem ast.

drills.translation: This is the very book I wanted.
drills.hint: the relative linker; the noun before it carries the indefinite ـی
drills.transliteration: in haman ketabi ast ke mikhastam.

points.title: Indirect speech with ke
points.function: Report what someone said
points.explanation: Reported speech is introduced by که, and — unlike English — Persian does NOT shift the tense backwards. گفت که می‌آید is literally "he said that he comes," but translates as "he said he was coming." Keep the tense the speaker actually used and let که do the work.

drills.hint: the linker that opens reported speech

drills.translation: He said he would come tomorrow.
drills.hint: comes — the tense stays as the speaker said it, no backshift

drills.sentence: من فکر می‌کنم {{answer}} او در خانه است.
drills.hint: the linker after a verb of thinking
drills.transliteration: man fekr mikonam ke u dar khane ast.

drills.hint: am — present kept in the report, where English shifts to "was"
drills.transliteration: u porsid ke man koja hastam.

drills.translation: I said I had read the book.
drills.hint: have read — the perfect, again unshifted

points.title: Ezafe chains: dar-e khane-ye dustam
points.function: Stack several linked nouns in a row
points.explanation: Ezafe links can chain: در خانهٔ دوستم is dar-e khane-ye dustam, "the door of the house of my friend." Each word in the chain carries an ezafe onto the next, and only the LAST element is the ultimate owner. Nothing is written after a consonant; after the silent ه the link appears as the hamza (خانهٔ), and after ا or و it appears as ی.

drills.translation: My friend's house door is open.
drills.hint: house — the middle link in the chain, carrying a written ezafe

drills.translation: My brother's book is on the table.
drills.hint: brother — the middle link between the thing and its owner
drills.transliteration: ketab-e baradar-e man ruye miz ast.

drills.hint: father — the middle link of the chain

drills.translation: My friend's father's car is red.
drills.hint: my friend — the last link, where the chain ends

drills.translation: The colour of the house door is white.
drills.hint: door — the middle link between "colour" and "house"

points.title: Infinitives as nouns: raftan, khandan
points.function: Use a verb as the subject or object of a sentence
points.explanation: The Persian infinitive (past stem + ن: رفتن، خواندن، نوشتن) doubles as a noun, covering English's "-ing" forms: خواندن کتاب خوب است ("reading books is good"), از رفتن می‌ترسم ("I'm afraid of going"). It takes ezafe, را and prepositions exactly like any other noun.

drills.hint: reading — the infinitive of the verb "to read", used as the subject
going — the infinitive as subject
writing — the infinitive of the verb "to write", linked to فارسی by ezafe

drills.translation: Running is good for your health.
drills.hint: running — the infinitive of the verb "to run"
reading — an infinitive can even take را as an object

points.title: tavanestan: saying what you can do
points.function: Say what is and isn't possible
points.explanation: توانستن ("to be able") is conjugated normally and is followed by a SUBJUNCTIVE, not an infinitive: می‌توانم بروم, literally "I can I-go." Both verbs carry the person. The negative is نمی‌توانم, and the past is توانستم / نتوانستم.

drills.hint: can — 1st person singular; the second verb stays subjunctive
can't — the negative, 3rd person singular
do — the light verb of "to help," in the subjunctive
go — subjunctive after "we can," 1st person plural
couldn't — the negative past of this verb

points.title: Past perfect: rafte budam
points.function: Set one past event before another
points.explanation: The past perfect is the participle plus the past of بودن: رفته بودم ("I had gone"), دیده بودی، خورده بود، رفته بودیم. It marks the earlier of two past events — وقتی رسیدم، او رفته بود ("when I arrived, he had already left").

drills.translation: When I arrived, he had left.
drills.hint: gone — the participle; بود carries the tense

drills.sentence: من آن کتاب را پیشتر خوانده {{answer}}.
drills.translation: I had already read that book.
drills.hint: had — the past of بودن, 1st person singular
drills.transliteration: man an ketab ra pishtar khande budam.

drills.hint: seen — participle of دیدن
drills.transliteration: ma u ra pishtar dide budim.

drills.hint: had — 2nd person singular of بودن
had — 3rd person plural of بودن

points.title: Unreal conditionals: agar miraftam
points.function: Talk about what would have been
points.explanation: For a condition contrary to fact, BOTH halves go into the habitual past (می‌ + past): اگر پول داشتم، این خانه را می‌خریدم — "if I had money, I would buy this house." The same pattern also covers the past-unreal reading ("if I had had money, I would have bought…"); context decides which one English needs.

drills.sentence: اگر پول {{answer}}، این خانه را می‌خریدم.
drills.translation: If I had money, I would buy this house.
drills.hint: had — the past of داشتن, which takes no می
drills.transliteration: agar pul dashtam, in khane ra mikharidam.

drills.sentence: اگر وقت داشتم، به تو زنگ {{answer}}.
drills.translation: If I had time, I would call you.
drills.hint: would hit — the light verb of "to call," in the habitual past
drills.transliteration: agar vaght dashtam, be to zang mizadam.

drills.translation: If he had come, I would have been happy.
drills.hint: would become — habitual past of شدن

drills.translation: If you had gone, you would have seen him.
drills.hint: had gone — habitual past, 2nd person singular
drills.transliteration: agar to mirafti, u ra mididi.

drills.translation: If I had known, I would have told you.
drills.hint: would have told — habitual past of گفتن

points.title: Passive with shodan: neveshte shod
points.function: Say what was done, without saying who did it
points.explanation: The passive is the past participle plus شدن: نوشته شد ("it was written"), ساخته شد ("it was built"), خوانده می‌شود ("it is read"). Persian uses it far less than English and normally leaves the agent out altogether — if you want to name the doer, an active sentence is the natural choice.

drills.hint: written — the participle before شد
closed — participle of بستن

drills.sentence: این خانه ده سال پیش ساخته {{answer}}.
drills.translation: This house was built ten years ago.
drills.hint: became — the auxiliary that carries the passive
drills.transliteration: in khane dah sal pish sakhte shod.

drills.translation: This book is read a lot.
drills.hint: is becoming — the present of the passive auxiliary
sent — participle of فرستادن

points.title: Causatives in -andan (recognition)
points.function: Recognize "make someone do it" verbs
points.explanation: Persian builds a causative by adding ـاندن to a present stem: خندیدن ("to laugh") → خنداندن ("to make laugh"), رسیدن ("to arrive") → رساندن ("to bring/deliver"), فهمیدن ("to understand") → فهماندن ("to make understand"), خوردن ("to eat") → خوراندن ("to feed"). The present stem ends in ـان: می‌رسانم. Not every verb has one — treat the forms as vocabulary to recognize.

drills.hint: delivered — the causative of رسیدن, past tense
makes laugh — the causative of خندیدن, present
made understand — the causative of فهمیدن
drills.transliteration: u in ra be man fahmand.

drills.hint: fed — the causative of خوردن
deliver — the causative of رسیدن, 1st person present
drills.transliteration: man to ra be khane miresanam.

points.title: ta: purpose and until
points.function: Join two clauses with "so that" or "until"
points.explanation: تا does two jobs. With a following SUBJUNCTIVE it means "in order to / so that": به تهران رفتم تا او را ببینم. With an indicative — or a plain time phrase — it means "until": تا فردا صبر کن, منتظر ماندم تا او آمد. The mood of the second verb tells the two readings apart.

drills.sentence: به تهران رفتم {{answer}} او را ببینم.
drills.translation: I went to Tehran to see him.
drills.hint: so that — the linker before a subjunctive
drills.transliteration: be Tehran raftam ta u ra bebinam.

drills.translation: I'm studying so that I pass.
drills.hint: become — subjunctive of شدن after the purpose linker
until — the same word before a time phrase
came — a plain past here, so تا reads as "until"

drills.translation: Come early so we can go together.
drills.hint: so that — again followed by a subjunctive
drills.transliteration: zud bia ta ba ham beravim.

points.title: Written vs. colloquial Persian (recognition)
points.function: Tell the written standard from the spoken form
points.explanation: Written Persian and Tehrani speech differ systematically: می‌روم is said miram, می‌خواهم is mikham, می‌گوید is mige, آن is un, این is in, را is ro, است shrinks to a suffixed ـه. Everything here is written in the standard form — recognize the spoken equivalents when you hear them, but keep writing the full ones.

drills.hint: the written standard for what is said "miram"
the written standard for what is said "mikham"
"that" — written in full, though it is said "un"
"is" — the full written word, which speech reduces to a suffix
the written standard for what is said "mige"

points.title: Formal and administrative register
points.function: Read and write official Persian
points.explanation: Official Persian has its own vocabulary for ordinary verbs: گردید or گشت for شد, نمود for کرد, می‌باشد for است, جهت for برای, and ایشان with a PLURAL verb for a single respected person. فرمودن replaces گفتن and کردن in polite requests: تکمیل فرمایید. Style guides criticize می‌باشد, but you will meet it constantly in letters and forms.

drills.translation: This letter was sent to you.
drills.hint: became — the formal counterpart of شد
drills.transliteration: in name baraye shoma ersal gardid.

drills.hint: did — the formal counterpart of کردند, plural out of deference
is — the bureaucratic substitute for است
the polite verb that replaces کنید in requests
drills.transliteration: khaheshmand ast form ra takmil farmayid.

drills.sentence: {{answer}} اطلاعات بیشتر با ما تماس بگیرید.
drills.hint: for — the formal preposition that replaces برای
drills.transliteration: jahat-e ettelaat-e bishtar ba ma tamas begirid.

points.title: Arabic broken plurals in Persian (recognition)
points.function: Recognize the Arabic plurals used in formal Persian
points.explanation: Alongside ـها, formal Persian keeps Arabic "broken" plurals, which reshape the word instead of adding a suffix: کتاب → کتب, عالم → علما, خبر → اخبار, نکته → نکات, مقاله → مقالات, عضو → اعضا, شخص → اشخاص. They belong to written and elevated style; the plain ـها plural is always available and often preferable.

drills.hint: books — the Arabic plural of کتاب
news — the Arabic plural of خبر

drills.translation: The religious scholars were at this meeting.
drills.hint: scholars — the Arabic plural of عالم, carrying an ezafe
drills.transliteration: olama-ye din dar in jalase budand.

drills.translation: He has written a great many articles.
drills.hint: articles — the Arabic plural of مقاله
members — the Arabic plural of عضو, carrying an ezafe

points.title: Literary past forms: baraft, hami (recognition)
points.function: Read the past tense of older Persian prose
points.explanation: Classical and literary Persian prefixes بـ to a plain past verb for narrative colour: برفت ("he went"), بگفت ("he said"), بدید ("he saw") — same meaning as رفت، گفت، دید, just an older register. The particle همی marks a continuous past where modern Persian would use می‌: همی رفت = می‌رفت. Both are for reading, not for writing modern prose.

drills.translation: He went away and did not return.
drills.hint: went — the literary form of رفت, with its بـ prefix

drills.translation: The king said: it is so.
drills.hint: said — the literary form of گفت

drills.translation: He saw him and recognized him.
drills.hint: saw — the literary form of دید
rose — a literary verb of standing up
the old continuous particle that modern Persian writes as a prefix

points.title: Classical verse conventions (recognition)
points.function: Read Persian poetry on its own terms
points.explanation: Classical verse keeps forms that modern prose has dropped: بود is read bovad and can mean "is"; ز stands for از; ـند closes a plural predicate (پیکرند = "they are one body"); and word order bends freely to the metre. Two lines every Persian speaker knows: Ferdowsi's توانا بود هر که دانا بود ("whoever is wise is strong") and Saadi's بنی‌آدم اعضای یک پیکرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند.

drills.hint: strong/capable — the first word of the hemistich
drills.transliteration: tavana bovad har ke dana bovad.

drills.translation: Human beings are the members of one body. (Saadi)
drills.hint: members — an Arabic plural carrying an ezafe

drills.translation: for in creation they are of one essence. (Saadi)
drills.hint: they are of one jewel — noun plus the poetic plural predicate ending
drills.transliteration: ke dar afarinesh ze yek gowharand.

drills.hint: from — the one-letter poetic form of the ordinary preposition
is — read bovad in verse, where prose would use است

points.title: Idioms and light-verb nuance
points.function: Say it the way Persian says it
points.explanation: At this level the compound verbs stop being transparent. از دست دادن is "to lose," not "to give from the hand"; دلم تنگ شده is "I miss (someone)," literally "my heart has grown narrow"; سر در آوردن (از) is "to make sense of"; دست به کار شدن is "to get down to it"; باور کردن is "to believe." Learn each compound whole — the pieces will not add up.

drills.hint: gave — the light verb of the idiom meaning "to lose"
become — the participle in the idiom "my heart has grown narrow"

drills.translation: I didn't believe what he said.
drills.hint: didn't do — the negated light verb of "to believe"

drills.translation: I can't make sense of this.
drills.hint: don't bring — the negated light verb of "to figure out"
drills.transliteration: az in mozu sar dar nemiavaram.

drills.hint: hand — the fixed noun in the idiom for setting to work

points.title: Register shifting: deference and distance
points.function: Move between polite, neutral and intimate Persian
points.explanation: Persian grades politeness through the verb itself. Deferential: ایشان with a plural verb, فرمودن for گفتن, تشریف داشتن/آوردن for بودن/آمدن, بفرمایید as the all-purpose invitation. Neutral: شما plus a plural verb, ordinary vocabulary. Intimate: تو with a singular verb. The same message reshapes completely — چه فرمودید؟ / چه گفتید؟ / چی گفتی؟

drills.hint: said — the deferential verb that replaces گفتید
the all-purpose polite invitation, from the deferential verb
have — the second half of the polite phrase for "to be present"
come — plural verb for one respected person
go — singular verb, the intimate register
